notes.front: What is Scrum, in one sentence?
notes.back: A lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organisations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems.
notes.explanation: Everything in this deck is part of this framework. “Framework” matters: Scrum defines only the parts it needs and leaves the rest to the people using it.
notes.example: Like the rules of a sport: they fix the pitch, the players and the whistle, but not the tactics.

notes.front: What is empiricism, in one sentence?
notes.back: The idea that knowledge comes from experience, and that decisions are made on what is observed.
notes.explanation: Scrum is founded on it: rather than predicting everything up front, you try something, look at the result and decide.
notes.example: Like tasting a soup as you cook it, rather than trusting the recipe’s timings blindly.

notes.front: What is lean thinking, in one sentence?
notes.back: Thinking that reduces waste and focuses on the essentials.
notes.explanation: It is the second foundation of Scrum, next to empiricism.
notes.example: Like packing only what you will actually use on a trip.

notes.front: What is a Sprint, in one sentence?
notes.back: A fixed-length cycle of one month or less in which ideas are turned into value; the next starts as soon as one ends.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide calls Sprints the heartbeat of Scrum: all the other work happens inside them.
notes.example: Like back-to-back two-week cycles, each ending with something usable and a look at what to change.

notes.front: Scrum is founded on {{c1::empiricism and lean thinking}}.
notes.explanation: Empiricism: decide from what you observe. Lean thinking: reduce waste and focus on the essentials.

notes.front: What kind of approach does Scrum use to optimise predictability and control risk?
notes.explanation: Iterative means working in repeated cycles; incremental means each cycle adds to what already exists.

notes.front: What is the longest a Sprint can be?
notes.explanation: Sprints are fixed length, one month or less, to create consistency. Shorter Sprints give more learning cycles and limit risk.

notes.front: A new Sprint starts {{c1::immediately after}} the previous Sprint ends.
notes.explanation: There is no gap between Sprints: all the work, including planning and review, happens inside them.

notes.front: Does Scrum give detailed instructions for every practice a team uses?
notes.back: No. It is purposefully incomplete, defining only the parts needed to implement Scrum theory.
notes.explanation: Various processes, techniques and methods can be used within the framework; the Scrum Guide leaves them to the people using it.

notes.front: A manager asks a team to fix a detailed 12-month plan now and never revisit it. Which foundation of Scrum does this ignore?
notes.back: Empiricism: decisions should follow what is observed as the work unfolds.
notes.choices:
A) Empiricism
B) Lean thinking
C) Neither: Scrum works from a fixed plan
notes.choicesExplained: B: lean thinking is about reducing waste and focusing on essentials, not learning from results. C: in complex work, the Scrum Guide says only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decisions.
notes.explanation: Empiricism says knowledge comes from experience, so a plan that is never revisited cannot learn from it.

notes.front: A team plans the whole product, builds all of it, then delivers once at the end. Is that the iterative, incremental approach Scrum uses?
notes.back: No. That is one pass and one delivery; Scrum repeats short cycles that each add to the product.
notes.explanation: Scrum uses repeated cycles (iterative) that each add usable work (incremental) to optimise predictability and control risk.

notes.front: A team wants six-week Sprints so it can fit more work into each one. Is that allowed in Scrum?
notes.back: No. A Sprint is one month or less.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide warns that when a Sprint’s horizon is too long, its goal may become invalid, complexity may rise and risk may increase.

notes.front: What is the difference between empiricism and lean thinking?
notes.back: Empiricism: decide from what you observe. Lean thinking: cut waste and focus on the essentials.
notes.explanation: Scrum is founded on both, so both come up; they answer different questions.
notes.contrast: Empiricism is about how you know; lean thinking is about what you leave out.
